original_value: Objective: We observe the effects of in-vehicle system gesture-based interaction versus touch-based interaction on driver distraction and user experience. Background: Driver distraction is a major problem for traffic safety, as it is a contributing factor to a number of accidents. Visual distraction in particular has a highly negative impact on the driver. One possibility for reducing visual driver distraction is to use new forms of interaction in the vehicle, such as gesture-based interaction. Method: In this experiment, participants drove on a motorway or in a city scenario while using touch-based interaction or gesture-based interaction. Subjective data, such as acceptance and workload, and objective data, including glance behavior, were gathered. Results: As a result, participants rated their subjective impressions of safe driving as higher when using gesture-based interaction. More specifically, acceptance and attractiveness were higher, and workload was lower. The participants performed significantly fewer glances to the display and the glances were much shorter. Conclusion: Gestures are a positive alternative for in-vehicle interaction since effects on driver distraction are less significant when compared to touch-based interaction. Application: Potential application of this research includes interaction design of typical in-vehicle information and entertainment functions.

result.paraphrase: Objective: This study examines how gesture-based versus touch-based in-vehicle interaction affects driver distraction and user experience. Background: Driver distraction is a major traffic-safety issue and contributes to many accidents, with visual distraction having especially harmful effects. One way to reduce it is to introduce new interaction methods in vehicles, such as gestures. Method: Participants in this experiment drove either on a motorway or in a city scenario while using touch-based or gesture-based interaction. Both subjective measures, such as acceptance and workload, and objective measures, including glance behavior, were collected. Results: Participants reported feeling safer when using gesture-based interaction. Specifically, acceptance and attractiveness were higher, while workload was lower. They also made significantly fewer glances at the display, and those glances were much shorter. Conclusion: Gestures are a promising alternative for in-vehicle interaction because they have less pronounced effects on driver distraction than touch-based interaction. Application: This research may inform the design of common in-vehicle information and entertainment functions.
